q: Which of these is most likely real property when a house is sold?
options: A dishwasher built into the kitchen cabinets
A freestanding refrigerator plugged into the wall
Patio furniture on the back deck
An area rug in the living room
wrong: A freestanding appliance that simply plugs in is movable personal property unless the contract says otherwise.
Furniture is movable and not attached, so it is personal property.
A rug lying on the floor is not attached or adapted to the home; it is personal property.
why: A built-in dishwasher is attached and adapted to the home, so it is a fixture and part of the real property.
hook: If it moves, it's personal. If it's part of the place, it's real.

q: When a court decides whether an item is a fixture, which factor usually carries the most weight?
options: The intention of the person who attached it
How long the item has been in place
Whether the item can be seen from the street
wrong: Cost has nothing to do with whether something became part of the real estate.
Time in place is not one of the fixture tests.
Visibility is not a fixture test.
why: Intent of the person who attached the item, shown by how and why it was attached, is generally the most important fixture test.
hook: MARIA decides, and the I in MARIA speaks loudest.

q: A seller removes a chandelier that was wired into the dining room ceiling before closing. The purchase agreement does not mention it. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The chandelier is presumed a fixture that belongs to the buyer
The seller may keep it because the contract is silent
Light fixtures are always personal property
The buyer's only remedy is to cancel the sale
wrong: Silence in the contract means the normal rule applies: attached items are fixtures that transfer.
Hard-wired light fixtures are a classic example of fixtures, not personal property.
The buyer can ask for the item to be returned or for a credit; cancellation is not the only remedy.
why: An item wired into the structure is a fixture. Unless the contract excludes it, it transfers with the property.
hook: Wired in means it stays in.

q: Your seller tells you they plan to take the custom drapery rods and the wall-mounted TV when they move. What should the agent do?
options: Write the exclusions into the listing and make sure the purchase agreement excludes them
Tell the seller fixtures can be removed any time before closing
Say nothing until a buyer asks about them
Tell the seller they can never keep attached items
wrong: Attached items are presumed to transfer; removing them without a written exclusion can breach the contract.
Waiting invites a dispute. Exclusions should be clear from the start.
Sellers can keep attached items if the contract clearly excludes them.
why: Attached items are presumed fixtures. Excluding them in writing in the listing and the purchase agreement avoids a dispute.
hook: Want to keep it? Write it out.

q: A restaurant tenant bolted a walk-in cooler to the floor for its business. The lease is ending. Which is correct?
options: The tenant may remove it before the lease ends but must repair any damage
It became the landlord's property when it was bolted down
The tenant must leave it but may charge the landlord for it
It may be removed only with a court order
wrong: Trade fixtures do not become the landlord's property just because they are attached.
The tenant owns the cooler and may take it; there is no automatic sale to the landlord.
No court order is needed to remove trade fixtures on time.
why: Equipment a tenant installs for business is a trade fixture. It stays the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease ends, with damage repaired.
hook: Trade fixtures travel with the trade.

q: A tenant moves out and leaves its trade fixtures behind after the lease expires. What usually happens to them?
options: They must be sold at auction
wrong: The right to remove trade fixtures ends when the lease ends.
Auction is not the standard rule for abandoned trade fixtures.
The county has no claim to them.
why: Trade fixtures not removed by the end of the lease generally become the landlord's property by accession.
hook: Leave it behind, leave it to the landlord.

q: A tenant farmer's lease ends early, through no fault of the tenant, before the annual crop is ripe. The tenant's right to come back and harvest is called:
wrong: Accession is how an owner acquires things added to their property, not a tenant's harvest right.
Severance is detaching something from the land; it's not the harvest right itself.
Annexation is attaching personal property to land.
why: Emblements are annual crops produced by labor. A tenant whose tenancy ends early through no fault of their own may return to harvest them.
hook: Emblements: you planted it, you pick it.

q: Personal property can become real property when it is permanently attached to the land.
wrong: This is annexation, a core rule: attaching personal property can make it part of the real estate.
why: True. Annexation, such as building lumber into a house, turns personal property into real property.
hook: Attach it and it can become real.

q: A manufactured home is always classified as real property.
wrong: A manufactured home can be personal property. It generally becomes real property only when permanently affixed and handled as real property under state rules.
why: False. Classification depends on whether the home is permanently affixed and how state law treats it.
hook: On wheels, it's a vehicle. On a foundation, it may be real.

q: An owner cuts down standing timber and sells the logs. Turning the trees into personal property is called:
wrong: Annexation is the opposite: attaching personal property to land.
Accretion is land gradually added by water deposits.
Partition divides co-owned property.
why: Severance detaches something from the land and converts real property to personal property.
hook: Sever it and it's set free.

q: A seller agrees to sell their washer and dryer to the buyer outside the home sale. Which document transfers ownership of the appliances?
wrong: Deeds transfer real property, not personal property.
A quitclaim deed is still a deed for real property.
A lease transfers possession, not ownership.
why: Personal property is transferred with a bill of sale. Deeds transfer real property.
hook: Deeds for dirt. Bills for things.

q: Which characteristic of land explains why no two parcels are exactly alike?
wrong: Immobility means land can't be moved, not that every parcel differs.
Indestructibility means land itself can't be destroyed.
Scarcity is an economic characteristic about limited supply.
why: Uniqueness, also called nonhomogeneity, means every parcel differs at least in location.
hook: Land is I-I-U: immobile, indestructible, unique.

q: Identical homes sell for more on one side of a street because that side is zoned for a top-rated school. This illustrates:
wrong: Immobility explains why location matters, but the preference for a location is area preference.
Indestructibility is unrelated to price differences between locations.
Permanence of investment refers to the long payback of improvements.
why: Area preference, or situs, is the economic characteristic that people value some locations more than others.
hook: Location, location, situs.

q: A metes and bounds description must:
options: Begin and end at the point of beginning
wrong: Referencing a plat is the lot and block method.
Townships and sections belong to the rectangular survey system.
A street address is not part of a legal description.
why: A metes and bounds description must close by returning to the point of beginning.
hook: Metes and bounds must come home.

q: "Lot 14, Block 3 of the Desert Vista subdivision" is an example of which description method?
wrong: Metes and bounds uses distances and directions from a point of beginning.
Rectangular survey uses townships, ranges, and sections.
A monument description relies on physical markers, not a plat.
why: Lot and block refers to a lot on a subdivision plat recorded with the county.
hook: Lot and block points to the plat.

q: How many acres are in one section?
wrong: 160 acres is a quarter section.
36 is the number of sections in a township.
43,560 is the number of square feet in one acre.
why: A section is one square mile, which is 640 acres.

q: How many acres are in the NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of a section?
formula: Acres = 640 × each fraction in the description
why: Multiply 640 by each fraction: 640 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 40 acres.
hook: Read it backward, multiply forward.

q: How many acres are in the S 1/2 of the NW 1/4 of a section?
formula: Acres = 640 × each fraction in the description
hook: Read it backward, multiply forward.

q: Put these rectangular survey units in order from largest to smallest.
why: A township holds 36 sections; a section is 640 acres; a quarter section is 160; a quarter of that is 40.
hook: 6, 36, 640, then keep quartering.

q: A street address is a sufficient legal description for a deed.
wrong: Addresses change and don't define boundaries. A deed needs a legal description such as lot and block or metes and bounds.
why: False. A legal description must identify the exact boundaries; a street address does not.
hook: An address finds the mailbox, not the boundary.

q: A township in the rectangular survey system measures:
wrong: 1 mile by 1 mile is a section.
24 miles square is the size of a check (quadrangle) formed by guide meridians and correction lines.
640 acres is one section.
why: A township is 6 miles square and contains 36 sections.

q: A rectangular parcel measures 660 feet by 1,320 feet. How many acres is it?
hook: Square feet over 43,560 equals acres.

q: Which of these is a general lien?
wrong: A mortgage attaches only to the property it secures, so it is specific.
A property tax lien attaches to the taxed parcel only, so it is specific.
A mechanic's lien attaches to the property that was improved, so it is specific.
why: A judgment lien can attach to all of the debtor's property, which makes it a general lien.
hook: Judgments go general. Mortgages stay specific.

q: Which lien usually takes priority over all others, regardless of when it was recorded?
wrong: A first mortgage ranks by its recording date and still falls behind property taxes.
A judgment lien ranks by when it attaches and falls behind property taxes.
Mechanic's lien priority varies by state but generally falls behind property taxes.
why: Real property taxes and special assessments generally take first priority regardless of recording date.
hook: Taxes take the front seat.

q: In an easement appurtenant, the parcel that benefits from the easement is the:
wrong: The servient tenement is burdened, not benefited.
An easement in gross benefits a person or company, not a parcel.
A remainder estate relates to life estates, not easements.
why: The dominant tenement benefits; the servient tenement carries the burden.
hook: Dominant dines. Servient serves.

q: A power company's right to run lines across private lots is best described as:
wrong: An appurtenant easement benefits a neighboring parcel, not a company.
A license is revocable permission; utility rights are lasting interests.
An encroachment is an unauthorized intrusion, not a granted right.
why: An easement that benefits a person or company rather than a parcel is an easement in gross. Utility easements are the classic example.
hook: In gross goes to a person or company.

q: During escrow, your buyer's survey shows the neighbor's garage extends three feet onto the lot. What should the agent do?
options: Tell the buyer right away and recommend they get legal advice before removing contingencies
Tell the buyer it's minor and not worth mentioning to anyone
Ask the neighbor to sign a note giving up the land
Tell the buyer to move the property line markers
wrong: An encroachment can affect title and value. Hiding or minimizing it breaches the agent's duties.
Drafting legal documents to resolve title issues is legal work; the agent should refer it out.
Moving markers is never appropriate and could be unlawful.
why: This is an encroachment, which can affect title and value. Disclose it promptly and refer the buyer to an attorney or the title company.
hook: Survey surprise? Tell, then refer.

q: Which statement about a license to use land is correct?
options: It is personal permission that can usually be revoked
It runs with the land when the property is sold
It is a type of lien
It must be recorded to be valid
wrong: Running with the land describes an easement appurtenant, not a license.
A license secures no debt, so it is not a lien.
A license is informal permission and does not need to be recorded.
why: A license is a personal, revocable privilege. It is not an interest in the land.
hook: A license is a permission slip.

q: A parcel has no access to any road except across a neighbor's land. A court may create:
wrong: An easement in gross benefits a person or company, not a landlocked parcel.
A license is revocable and would not solve a permanent access problem.
A lis pendens is a notice of a pending lawsuit.
why: An easement by necessity gives a landlocked parcel access to a road.
hook: Landlocked? Necessity opens the gate.

q: When the dominant parcel is sold, the benefit of an easement appurtenant transfers to the buyer.
wrong: An easement appurtenant runs with the land and transfers automatically with either parcel.
why: True. Easements appurtenant run with the land, so the benefit passes to the new owner.
hook: Appurtenant attaches to the land, not the owner.

q: Every encumbrance is a lien.
wrong: Easements, deed restrictions, and encroachments are encumbrances that are not liens. Every lien is an encumbrance, but not the other way around.
why: False. All liens are encumbrances, but many encumbrances, like easements, are not liens.
hook: All liens encumber; not all encumbrances are liens.

q: A property is sold at foreclosure. Put these claims in the usual order of payment, first to last.
why: Property taxes come first. The remaining liens are generally paid in the order they were recorded.
hook: Taxes take the front seat. Everyone else lines up by recording date.

q: A recorded notice warning that a lawsuit affecting title to a property is pending is called a:
wrong: A mechanic's lien secures payment for work or materials.
A writ of execution orders the sale of property to satisfy a judgment.
A satisfaction shows a debt has been paid off.
why: A lis pendens gives public notice that title is in dispute in a pending lawsuit.
hook: Lis pendens: lawsuit pending.

q: Which estate gives the owner the greatest interest in real property?
wrong: A life estate ends when the measuring life ends.
A determinable fee can be lost if its condition is broken.
An estate for years is a leasehold, not ownership.
why: Fee simple absolute is unlimited in duration, inheritable, and has no conditions.
hook: Absolute means no strings.

q: A deed grants land to the city "so long as the land is used as a public park." The city holds a:
wrong: An absolute fee has no conditions; this one does.
A life estate is measured by a person's life, not a use.
A leasehold is a tenant's interest under a lease.
why: "So long as" language creates a fee simple determinable, which ends automatically if the use stops.
hook: "So long as" snaps back.

q: Maria deeds her home "to Ben for life, then to Carla." Carla is the:
wrong: Ben is the life tenant.
Maria is the grantor.
A reversion would go back to Maria; Carla is a third party.
why: A third party who receives the property when a life estate ends is the remainderman.
hook: Remainder goes forward.

q: Juan deeds a cabin "to Ana for life" and says nothing more. When Ana dies, the cabin:
options: Reverts to Juan or his heirs
Becomes owned by the tenants in possession
wrong: Ana's interest ended at her death, so there is nothing for her heirs to inherit.
The state takes property only by escheat when there are no heirs.
Tenants have no ownership claim from a life estate ending.
why: With no remainderman named, the property reverts to the grantor or the grantor's heirs.
hook: Reversion goes back.

q: A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant is a:
options: Fee simple subject to condition subsequent
wrong: A conventional life estate is created by the owner and is usually measured by the life tenant's own life.
A legal life estate is created by law, not by the measuring life.
That is a defeasible fee, not a life estate.
why: Pur autre vie means "for the life of another."
hook: Autre means other.

q: Which action is a life tenant NOT allowed to take?
options: Tear out the plumbing and let the house deteriorate
Rent the home to a tenant
wrong: A life tenant may lease the property for the length of the life estate.
A life tenant may sell their interest, which lasts only as long as the measuring life.
Living there is the core of a life estate.
why: A life tenant may not commit waste, meaning damage that harms the remainderman's or reversioner's future interest.
hook: Use it, don't ruin it.

q: A lease runs from June 1, 2026, to May 31, 2027. This tenant holds a(n):
wrong: A periodic tenancy renews automatically, such as month to month.
A tenancy at will has no fixed term.
Sufferance applies only to a holdover without consent.
why: Any lease with a definite start and end date is an estate for years, even if it is shorter than a year.
hook: Years ends itself.

q: A tenant stays after the lease expires without the landlord's consent. This is a:
wrong: A tenancy at will requires the landlord's consent.
A periodic tenancy requires agreement and renews by period.
The estate for years already ended.
why: A holdover without consent is a tenancy at sufferance.
hook: Sufferance is uninvited.

q: A leasehold estate is a type of freehold estate.
wrong: Leaseholds are non-freehold estates: the tenant has possession, not ownership.
why: False. Freehold estates are ownership estates. Leaseholds are non-freehold estates held by tenants.
hook: Owners hold freeholds. Tenants hold leaseholds.

q: A life tenant may sell the life estate, but the buyer's interest ends when the measuring life ends.
wrong: The life tenant can sell only what they own, and that interest ends with the measuring life.
why: True. You can only sell what you own, and a life estate ends with the measuring life.
hook: You can sell your time, not more of it.

q: A month-to-month rental that continues until either party gives notice is a(n):
wrong: An estate for years has a fixed end date.
Sufferance means the tenant stays without consent.
A life estate is a freehold measured by a life.
why: A periodic tenancy renews automatically for successive periods until proper notice is given.
hook: Periodic repeats.

q: Ownership of real property by one person alone is called ownership in:
wrong: Joint tenancy requires two or more owners.
Tenancy in common requires two or more owners.
A partnership is a business with two or more partners.
why: Severalty means sole ownership, "severed" from anyone else.
hook: Severalty is solo.

q: The four unities required to create a joint tenancy are:
wrong: Income and taxes are not unities.
Purpose and transfer are not unities.
Price and terms are contract terms, not unities.
why: Joint tenants must take equal interests, at the same time, by the same document, with equal right of possession.
hook: PITT.

q: A tenant in common dies with a will. Their interest:
options: Passes under their will to their devisees
Passes automatically to the other co-owners
wrong: Automatic passage to co-owners is survivorship, which belongs to joint tenancy.
Reversion applies to life estates, not co-ownership.
The interest survives the owner and passes to their estate.
why: Tenancy in common has no right of survivorship, so the interest passes by will or to heirs.
hook: Common shares go to your people.

q: Ana, Ben, and Cy own a lot as joint tenants. Ana sells her interest to Dee. What is the result?
options: Dee is a tenant in common with a 1/3 share; Ben and Cy remain joint tenants as to 2/3
Dee becomes a joint tenant with Ben and Cy
The whole joint tenancy becomes a tenancy in common
The sale is void without Ben's and Cy's consent
wrong: Dee received her interest at a different time and by a different deed, so the unities are broken for her share.
Only the transferred share loses the unities; Ben and Cy still share all four.
A joint tenant may sell their interest without consent.
why: Selling breaks the unities for that share only. The buyer becomes a tenant in common, and the remaining joint tenants keep survivorship between themselves.
hook: PITT: break a unity, break the survivorship.

q: Co-owners cannot agree on whether to sell. A court action to divide the property or order it sold is a:
wrong: Quiet title resolves competing claims to title.
Foreclosure enforces a lien after a default.
Condemnation is the government taking property by eminent domain.
why: Partition lets a court divide co-owned property or order a sale and split the proceeds.
hook: Can't agree? Partition.

q: Which form of co-ownership allows the owners to hold unequal shares?
wrong: Joint tenancy requires equal interests (unity of interest).
Tenancy by the entirety is for married couples who hold as one unit.
Severalty has only one owner.
why: Tenants in common can hold unequal undivided interests, such as 60/40.
hook: Common shares can be uneven.

q: In a trust, who holds legal title to the property?
wrong: The trustor creates the trust and transfers the property into it.
The beneficiary receives the benefits but does not hold legal title.
The recorder records documents but holds no title.
why: The trustee holds legal title and manages the property for the beneficiary.
hook: Trustor sets it up. Trustee holds it. Beneficiary enjoys it.

q: A corporation that owns real property holds title as:
options: Tenants in common with its shareholders
wrong: Shareholders own stock, not the real estate.
Directors manage the company but don't own its property.
A corporation's ownership isn't measured by a life.
why: A corporation is a single legal entity, so it owns property in severalty.
hook: One entity, one owner.

q: A joint tenant can leave their interest to an heir by will.
wrong: Right of survivorship passes the interest to the surviving joint tenants at the moment of death, before a will can act on it.
why: False. Survivorship controls, so the interest passes to the surviving joint tenants.
hook: Survivorship beats the will.

q: In a limited partnership, limited partners generally risk only the amount they invested.
wrong: Limited partners' liability is limited to their investment; the general partner carries full liability.
why: True. Limited partners are passive investors with limited liability.
hook: Limited partner, limited risk.

q: Which entity gives its owners limited personal liability and can be taxed as a pass-through entity?
wrong: General partners are personally liable for partnership debts.
A sole proprietor is personally liable for all business debts.
Joint tenancy is a form of co-ownership, not a business entity.
why: An LLC combines limited liability with flexible, often pass-through, taxation.
hook: LLC: limited liability, less corporate double tax.

q: A condominium owner owns:
options: The unit in fee simple plus an undivided interest in the common elements
Shares in a corporation plus a proprietary lease
A right to use the unit one week each year
Only the interior paint and fixtures
wrong: Shares and a proprietary lease describe a cooperative.
A recurring week describes a timeshare.
Condo owners own the unit itself, not just its finishes.
why: Condo ownership is fee title to the unit plus a shared undivided interest in the common elements.
hook: Condo: own the box, share the rest.

q: A buyer purchasing in a cooperative receives:
options: Shares in the corporation and a proprietary lease
wrong: Co-op buyers don't get a deed; the corporation owns the building.
An easement in gross benefits a person or company; it isn't co-op ownership.
A timeshare estate is ownership of a time interval.
why: In a co-op, the corporation owns the building. Buyers get shares and a proprietary lease.
hook: Co-op: you own stock, not a unit.

q: A balcony that only one condo unit can use is an example of a:
wrong: General common elements, like the lobby, are for all owners.
The balcony is not part of the unit itself in most declarations; it is reserved for it.
Trade fixtures are a commercial tenant's equipment.
why: Limited common elements are owned in common but reserved for the use of one or some units.
hook: Limited: shared ownership, private use.

q: A condominium is legally created when the developer records a:
wrong: A proprietary lease belongs to cooperatives.
A bill of sale transfers personal property.
A lis pendens is notice of a lawsuit.
why: Recording the declaration creates the condominium and its common elements.
hook: Declare it to create it.

q: In a planned unit development (PUD), owners typically own:
options: Their lot and home, while the association owns the common areas
Only the airspace inside their unit
A right to use a unit for a set week
wrong: Shares describe a cooperative.
Airspace ownership describes a condominium unit.
A set week describes a timeshare.
why: PUD owners hold title to their lot and home. The association owns and maintains the common areas.
hook: PUD: your dirt, their park.

q: Which risk is greater for a cooperative owner than for a condominium owner?
options: Other shareholders' failure to pay can leave the remaining owners covering the blanket mortgage
The owner cannot get a separate tax bill for the common areas
The owner must pay HOA assessments
The owner cannot sell their interest
wrong: Condo owners don't get separate tax bills for common areas either; this isn't a co-op specific risk.
Both condo and co-op owners pay association charges.
Co-op shares can be sold, often with board approval.
why: A co-op usually has one blanket mortgage and shared expenses. When some owners default, the rest may have to cover the shortfall.
hook: Co-op: one loan, everyone's problem.

q: What is the key difference between a timeshare estate and a timeshare use?
options: A timeshare estate is a real property ownership interest; a timeshare use is only a right to use
A timeshare use is always permanent; an estate expires
Only a timeshare use can be sold
wrong: A timeshare use typically lasts for a set number of years; it is the estate that is an ownership interest.
Timeshare estates can be sold like other real property interests.
The difference matters: one is ownership, the other is a right of use.
why: A timeshare estate conveys a real property interest. A timeshare use gives only the right to occupy for a period.
hook: A timeshare estate owns a slice of time. A timeshare use rents it.

q: A buyer asks whether the condo association is planning a special assessment. What should the agent do?
options: Help the buyer get and review the association documents, including the budget, reserves and meeting minutes, and direct the question to the association
Assure the buyer there won't be one
Tell the buyer special assessments only apply to commercial buildings
Tell the buyer it doesn't matter because assessments are tax deductible
wrong: Guessing about future assessments could be a misrepresentation.
Residential associations can levy special assessments.
Homeowner assessments on a personal residence are generally not deductible, and the question still deserves a real answer.
why: The facts are in the association's documents. Help the buyer get them and avoid guessing.
hook: Don't guess. Get the documents.

q: Each condominium unit is taxed separately.
wrong: Each condo unit is a separate parcel with its own tax bill, which includes its share of the common elements.
why: True. Each unit is a separate parcel with its own tax assessment.
hook: Own the box, own the bill.

q: In a cooperative, each resident typically receives a deed to their apartment.
wrong: Co-op residents own shares in the corporation and hold a proprietary lease; the corporation holds the deed.
why: False. The corporation owns the building; residents hold shares and a proprietary lease.
hook: Co-op: stock, not a deed.

q: A condo owner stops paying association assessments. What can the association generally do?
options: Place a lien on the owner's unit
Evict the owner like a tenant
Take ownership of the unit without any process
wrong: An owner isn't a tenant, so eviction doesn't apply.
Ownership can't be taken without legal process.
Assessments are mandatory under the declaration.
why: Unpaid assessments can become a lien on the unit, which the association may enforce.
hook: Skip the dues, risk a lien.
